title: The Digestive System
intro: The digestive system, also called the gastrointestinal (GI) system, is a hollow tube from the mouth to the anus plus a few helper organs. It breaks food down, absorbs the nutrients and water, and gets rid of the waste.

sections.title: Nutrients and the GI system

steps.title: What you should be able to do
bullets: Describe the parts and jobs of the GI tract and the accessory organs, and how food enters and moves through the tract.
Contrast how different nutrients are digested and absorbed, explain what the gut microbiome does, and describe where the GI system comes from in the embryo.

steps.title: Why we need nutrients
bullets: The body needs **nutrients** for growth, reproduction and keeping the inside of the body steady (homeostasis).
The gastrointestinal (GI) system **digests** food, which means it processes it, and then absorbs the nutrients and water.

steps.title: Essential nutrients
bullets: Some nutrients are **essential**: they can only be obtained in the diet.
Essential fatty acids (linoleic acid, linolenic acid) and essential amino acids (histidine, isoleucine, methionine) are on the list.
So are vitamins (humans can make only vitamin D) and minerals such as iron, sodium, iodine, zinc, manganese and molybdenum.

steps.title: A hollow tube
bullets: The GI system mainly consists of the **alimentary canal**, also called the **gastrointestinal tract**.
This hollow tube through the body essentially makes humans doughnut-shaped. The space inside the tube is the **lumen**.
The tract has different jobs along its length: mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus.

img.alt: A human body with the digestive organs drawn inside and each organ and accessory organ labelled with its jobs.

steps.title: Organs and accessory organs
bullets: The **accessory organs** are the salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas. They are not part of the tube, but they are important.
They add their products to the tract. For example, bile and pancreatic juice reach the duodenum through ducts.
The picture lists the jobs of each organ. The appendix has no known digestive function.

boxes.text: Why is the human body called doughnut-shaped? The GI tract is a hollow tube that runs right through the body, so the body is like a doughnut and the lumen is the hole.
Think of the tract as a one-way tunnel: food goes in at the mouth and the leftovers come out at the anus. Accessory organs are the helpers beside the tunnel that pour in juices.

Humans can synthesize only vitamin D themselves (slide 2), but gut microbes make vitamins K, B6 and biotin (slide 25). Do not mix up 'the body makes it' with 'gut bacteria make it'. Slide 3 says the GI system 'principally' consists of the tract; the accessory organs (salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas) are NOT part of the tube.

sourceNotes: Slides 1-5. Slide 1 lists the learning objectives, slide 2 dietary necessities, slide 3 organization, slide 4 the labelled organ figure, slide 5 an overview picture with the caption: Digestion takes place in the alimentary canal, also called the digestive tract or gastrointestinal tract.
Slide 2: homeostasis gloss 'keeping the inside of the body steady' is a plain-language addition (outside source).
Trick box analogy (one-way tunnel) is outside source.

sections.title: The four layers of the GI wall

img.alt: A cut-away tube showing the lumen, the mucosa and submucosa on the inside and the muscle layers and serosa outside it.

steps.title: Mucosa and submucosa
bullets: The wall of the GI tract has **four layers** that are the same all along the tract.
The **mucosa** is the innermost layer, a mucous membrane that touches the lumen.
The **submucosa** is connective tissue that holds the blood vessels, lymph vessels and nerves.

img.alt: The same cut-away tube with the muscularis and serosa highlighted; the circular and longitudinal muscle layers are labelled.

steps.title: Muscularis and serosa
bullets: The **muscularis** has several layers of smooth muscle. It makes food move through the tract (motility).
The **serosa** is the outermost connective tissue layer. It anchors the GI tract to the wall of the body cavity through the **mesentery**.
Thick muscular rings called **sphincters** separate some organs along the tract.
Four layers from the lumen outward: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, serosa.

boxes.text: Each layer has its own job: the mucosa lines the tube, the submucosa carries blood, lymph and nerves, the muscularis squeezes food along, and the serosa holds the tube in place. Because the muscle is in the wall, damage to the muscularis would mainly affect the movement of food.
From the lumen outward the layers spell a chant: Mucosa, Submucosa, Muscularis, Serosa. Try 'Many Students Make Soup' (M, S, M, S), where the first M is nearest the food.

Slide 6 says 'fours layers' (a typo): there are FOUR. The picture on slides 6-7 says the muscularis has 'two layers of smooth muscle' (circular and longitudinal), but the stomach picture on slide 12 also shows an oblique layer, and the text only says 'multiple layers'. Do not state a fixed number of muscle layers.

sourceNotes: Slides 6-7 (same figure, with a different layer boxed on each slide).
Box analogy 'Many Students Make Soup' is a memory aid made for this site (outside source).

images.alt: A cut-away tube showing the lumen, the mucosa and submucosa on the inside and the muscle layers and serosa outside it.
The same cut-away tube with the muscularis and serosa highlighted; the circular and longitudinal muscle layers are labelled.

sections.title: Moving and mixing food

img.alt: Three steps showing a ball of food squeezed down the esophagus and into the stomach by muscle contractions behind it.

steps.title: Peristalsis pushes food on
bullets: **Peristalsis** pushes a ball of food (a **bolus**) forward.
The muscle in front of the bolus relaxes while the muscle behind it contracts. The squeeze pushes the bolus on.
In the picture the bolus travels down the esophagus and into the stomach.

img.alt: Three views of an intestine wall pinching in several places at once so the food is split into small moving pockets.

steps.title: Segmentation mixes food
bullets: **Segmentation** mixes food instead of moving it forward.
Sections of smooth muscle relax and contract at random, which makes a back-and-forth mixing motion.
The mixing presses food against the mucosa, which makes it possible to absorb nutrients.
The smooth muscle of the GI tract makes two kinds of motility: peristalsis (pushes food forward) and segmentation (mixes food).

boxes.text: To push something forward you need a squeeze behind it and open space ahead of it. That is why the muscle behind the bolus contracts while the muscle in front relaxes. Mixing helps absorption because it keeps pressing food against the mucosa.
P for Push, S for Stir: Peristalsis Pushes the bolus forward, Segmentation Stirs it back and forth against the wall. Like squeezing toothpaste along a tube versus swirling soup in a bowl.

The most common swap: segmentation does NOT push food forward, and peristalsis does NOT mix. Slide 8: peristalsis = propels, segmentation = mixes. Peristalsis also happens in the stomach (slide 13), where it churns the contents.

sourceNotes: Slide 8. The text says the smooth muscle produces two kinds of motility, peristalsis and segmentation.
Trick box toothpaste/soup analogy is outside source.

images.alt: Three steps showing a ball of food squeezed down the esophagus and into the stomach by muscle contractions behind it.
Three views of an intestine wall pinching in several places at once so the food is split into small moving pockets.

sections.title: The mouth and swallowing

img.alt: The upper and lower rows of adult teeth with the four tooth types labelled, and a cut-through tooth with its parts labelled.

steps.title: Chewing and teeth
bullets: Chewing (**mastication**) starts digestion in the mouth. This is **mechanical digestion**, the physical breaking up of food.
Adult teeth come in four types: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars.
A tooth has a crown above the gum and a root in the bone. The picture labels enamel, dentin, pulp cavity, root canal and the periodontal ligament.

img.alt: A side view of the skull and jaw showing the parotid, sublingual and submandibular salivary glands.

steps.title: Saliva and salivary glands
bullets: Three pairs of **exocrine** salivary glands (parotid, sublingual and submandibular) secrete saliva into the mouth.
Saliva contains **salivary amylase**, which digests starch. This is **chemical digestion**.
Saliva also moistens food, maintains pH with bicarbonate and inhibits bacteria with lysozyme.

img.alt: A side view of the head showing the tongue pushing a ball of food back into the pharynx while the esophagus stays closed.

steps.title: Voluntary phase of swallowing
bullets: Swallowing has two phases: **voluntary** and **involuntary**.
In the voluntary phase the tongue pushes the bolus into the pharynx while the esophagus stays closed.
The pharynx is the passageway for both food and air.

img.alt: A side view of the head showing the soft palate raised and the epiglottis bent down so food is guided into the esophagus.

steps.title: Involuntary phase of swallowing
bullets: The soft palate rises to close the passage to the nasal cavity.
The epiglottis bends to close the trachea (the airway) and open the esophagus at the same time.
The bolus then moves down the esophagus to the stomach. The **esophageal sphincter** separates the two.

boxes.text: The pharynx carries both food and air. So during the automatic phase the soft palate shuts off the nose and the epiglottis shuts off the trachea while opening the esophagus. This sends the bolus down toward the stomach and not into the airway.
Voluntary = you choose it: your tongue pushes the food back. Involuntary = it happens by itself: palate up, epiglottis down, food goes down the esophagus.

Slide 10 says the soft palate rises 'while' the epiglottis bends 'simultaneously', but the picture numbers them 3 and 4. Do not memorize a strict order between those two. Also, amylase appears twice: salivary amylase (mouth) and pancreatic amylase (small intestine) both digest starch.

sourceNotes: Slides 9-10. The tooth counts (incisors 8, canines 4, premolars 8, molars 12) and the gland names (parotid, sublingual, submandibular) come from labels on the slide 9 figure. Saliva functions (moistens food, bicarbonate maintains pH, amylase digests starch, lysozyme inhibits bacteria) come from the slide 4 figure.
Slide 10 step 2 'muscles keep the esophagus closed' is on the figure. The soft palate / epiglottis timing is ambiguous (text says simultaneously, figure numbers 3 then 4).

'mechanical digestion = physical breaking up of food' is a plain-language gloss (outside source). Trick box wording is outside source. 'Exocrine' means the glands release their product out through ducts (outside source gloss).

A side view of the skull and jaw showing the parotid, sublingual and submandibular salivary glands.

sections.title: The stomach

img.alt: A slice of the stomach wall with its layers on the left and a close-up of a gastric pit with mucus, acid and pepsinogen secreting cells on the right.

steps.title: Gastric pits and their cells
bullets: The stomach lining (mucosa) has deep **gastric pits**. Cells there secrete the parts of **gastric juice**.
Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. Mucous neck cells secrete mucus. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen.
The stomach wall has the same four layers as the rest of the tract.

steps.title: What each secretion does
bullets: **Hydrochloric acid** is highly acidic (about pH 2) and breaks down large bits of food. **Intrinsic factor** helps the small intestine absorb vitamin B₁₂.
**Mucus** (mucin) protects the stomach lining from being damaged by the acid.
**Pepsinogen** is converted into pepsin in the low-pH stomach, and pepsin begins protein digestion.

img.alt: Four views of the stomach showing waves of muscle contraction pushing the contents toward the pyloric sphincter and back.

steps.title: Churning in the stomach
bullets: Peristalsis in the stomach churns its contents. The **pyloric sphincter** at the exit is the reason.
Only some **chyme** slowly leaks through the pyloric sphincter into the small intestine.
The lower esophageal sphincter at the entrance is also labelled in the picture.

boxes.text: Pepsinogen is made in an inactive form and only becomes pepsin in the low-pH stomach, so protein digestion starts where the acid is. The pyloric sphincter at the exit means waves of peristalsis push the contents against it and they bounce back, which churns and mixes the food.
Match the cell to its product: Parietal = acid (and intrinsic factor), Mucous neck = mucus, Chief = the chief enzyme precursor, pepsinogen.

Parietal cells make TWO things (hydrochloric acid AND intrinsic factor, slide 11). Pepsinogen comes from chief cells, not parietal cells, and mucus from mucous neck cells. The slides do not define 'chyme' (the stomach contents that leak into the small intestine); the plain-language meaning is an addition.

sourceNotes: Slides 11-13. Slide 12 picture labels: mucus, gastric pits, mucus-secreting cells, acid-secreting cell, pepsinogen-secreting cell, stomach wall layers (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis with oblique, circular and longitudinal layers, serosa).

Slide 13: 'Peristalsis in the stomach causes a churning ... due to the presence of the pyloric sphincter'. The explanation that contents are pushed against the closed exit and bounce back, and 'chyme' as the stomach contents, are plain-language glosses (outside source); the slide 13 figure shows red arrows toward and back from the pyloric sphincter. Slide 4: stomach stores and mixes food.
Trick box (chief = chief enzyme precursor) is outside source.

images.alt: A slice of the stomach wall with its layers on the left and a close-up of a gastric pit with mucus, acid and pepsinogen secreting cells on the right.
Four views of the stomach showing waves of muscle contraction pushing the contents toward the pyloric sphincter and back.

sections.title: The small intestine

steps.title: Digestion and absorption
bullets: The small intestine does both **digestion** and **absorption**. About 90% of food is absorbed in the small intestine.
It neutralizes stomach acid, adds digestive enzymes and bile, and breaks proteins, carbohydrates and lipids into absorbable materials.
It has three parts: the **duodenum** (where most digestion occurs), then the **jejunum** and the ileum (both for absorption).

img.alt: A zoom from a folded intestine wall to villi, to one villus with its blood and lymph vessels, to a single cell covered in microvilli.

steps.title: Folds, villi and microvilli
bullets: The wall has large folds covered in tiny **villi**. Villi are made of epithelial cells that are covered in **microvilli** (cytoplasmic projections).
Each villus has blood vessels (an arteriole and a venule) and a central lymph vessel called the **lacteal**.
Folds, villi and microvilli together give a much larger surface area for absorption.

img.alt: The lining of a small intestine with damaged flat villi on the left and normal finger-like villi on the right.

steps.title: Celiac disease
bullets: In **celiac disease**, gluten proteins bind to mutated antigen-presenting receptors. This triggers an immune response and inflammation in the small intestine.
The villi are damaged and shrink (atrophy). With less absorbing surface, the body suffers general malabsorption and nutrient deficiency.
About 1% of people have it. The only treatment is a gluten-free diet.
Duodenum = most digestion; jejunum and ileum = absorption; about 90% of food is absorbed in the small intestine.

boxes.text: Nutrients are absorbed through the surface of the lining. Folds on folds on tiny projections pack a huge surface into a short tube, so more food can be absorbed. In celiac disease the villi shrink, the surface area falls, and that is why nutrient deficiency follows.
D for Digestion in the Duodenum; the other two parts, Jejunum and Ileum, are for absorption. The order along the tube is D, J, I.

Slide 14 says about 90% of food is absorbed in the small intestine, yet the duodenum is labelled as 'where most digestion occurs' and only the jejunum and ileum are labelled 'absorption'. Do not answer that the duodenum is the main absorbing part. Slide 4 says the small intestine 'absorbs most of the water and nutrients' and the large intestine 'absorbs the last' of them.

sourceNotes: Slides 14-16. Slide 15 figure labels: folds, villi, mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, serosa, epithelial cell, lacteal, mucus-producing cell, arteriole, venule, lymph vessel, microvilli. Slide 16 figure: damaged villi (celiac) vs normal villi.

'Folds, villi and microvilli give a larger surface area' is stated on slide 14. Linking the shrunken villi to less surface area and so to malabsorption is a logical link between slides 14 and 16 (partly outside source).
Trick box D, J, I is outside source.

images.alt: A zoom from a folded intestine wall to villi, to one villus with its blood and lymph vessels, to a single cell covered in microvilli.
The lining of a small intestine with damaged flat villi on the left and normal finger-like villi on the right.

sections.title: Accessory organs and digestive enzymes

img.alt: The liver, gallbladder, pancreas, stomach and duodenum with the bile duct and pancreatic duct and each organ's jobs labelled.

steps.title: Liver, gallbladder and pancreas
bullets: The **liver** produces bile. The **gallbladder** stores and concentrates the bile and delivers it to the duodenum through the common bile duct.
The **pancreas** secretes enzymes (proteases, amylase, lipase) and sodium bicarbonate, and delivers them to the duodenum through ducts.
Bile contains water and electrolytes, cholesterol, bile salts, lecithin and pigments.

steps.title: The pancreas has two jobs
bullets: The pancreas is a gland with an **endocrine** function (regulating blood glucose) and an **exocrine** function (secreting pancreatic juice).
It secretes sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃), which neutralizes stomach acid.
Its enzymes: trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase digest proteins; pancreatic amylase digests starch; lipase digests lipids; pancreatic nucleases digest DNA and RNA.

img.alt: A table listing each digestive enzyme with where it is made, where it works, what it digests and what it produces.

steps.title: Major digestive enzymes
bullets: Carbohydrates: amylases (salivary and pancreatic) turn polysaccharides into disaccharides, and maltase turns disaccharides into monosaccharides such as glucose.
Proteins: pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin make peptides; carboxypeptidase and intestinal enzymes make amino acids.
Lipase makes free fatty acids and monoglyceride from triglycerides. Pancreatic nucleases and nucleosidases break down DNA and RNA.

img.alt: The liver and digestive organs with the hepatic portal vein, drawn in blue, collecting blood from the stomach, pancreas and intestines and carrying it to the liver.

steps.title: Bile and the hepatic portal system
bullets: Bile **emulsifies** lipids into micelles, which eases digestion by lipase.
The **hepatic portal system** drains blood from the digestive tract to the liver.
The liver also stores, synthesizes and processes chemicals (for example in fat metabolism). The gallbladder concentrates and stores bile.

boxes.text: Stomach acid arrives in the duodenum, and sodium bicarbonate from the pancreas helps neutralize it. Bile salts break big fat globules into tiny emulsion droplets, which eases fat digestion by lipase. Micelles form later, after lipase has digested the fats.
Enzyme names tell you the job: amylase = starch, lipase = lipids, nucleases = DNA and RNA, and the protein cutters are pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase.

Same nutrient, different place: salivary amylase works in the mouth, pancreatic amylase in the small intestine (slide 19). Pepsin is the only major enzyme made AND active in the stomach. Lipase comes from the pancreas, not the liver or gallbladder; bile only emulsifies. Maltase works on disaccharides, not on polysaccharides. Intestinal enzymes are listed under protein digestion (peptides to amino acids).

sourceNotes: Slides 17-20. Slide 17 figure (liver, gallbladder, pancreas) lists the bile contents. Slide 19 is Table 14.1 'Major enzymes of digestion' (copied into the table here). Slide 20 figure: hepatic portal vein.

Why box: bile gives lipase more surface and sodium bicarbonate helping neutralize acid arriving in the duodenum are plain-language links (outside source). Slide 14 says the small intestine neutralizes stomach acid and slide 18 says sodium bicarbonate neutralizes stomach acid.
Trick box wording is outside source.

sections.title: Large intestine and absorption

img.alt: The large intestine with the cecum, appendix, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anus and anal sphincters labelled.

steps.title: The large intestine
bullets: The **large intestine** absorbs nutrients and water and temporarily stores and eliminates waste.
Its parts are the **cecum** (with the appendix), the **colon** (ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid), the rectum and the anus.
Two anal sphincters separate the anus from the outside. The internal one is smooth muscle and the external one is skeletal muscle.

img.alt: A cell layer lining the intestine with carbohydrates and proteins digested outside it and amino acids and sugars crossing the cells into a capillary.

steps.title: Absorbing amino acids and sugars
bullets: Amino acids and monosaccharides cross the epithelial cells by **active transport**.
They then enter the capillary and travel toward the hepatic portal system, which leads to the liver.
Water is absorbed by **osmosis**. Vitamins and minerals are absorbed by various means, depending on whether they are water-soluble or fat-soluble.

img.alt: Seven numbered steps of fat digestion from fat globules and bile salts to chylomicrons entering the lacteal.

steps.title: Absorbing fats
bullets: Bile salts break fat globules into emulsion droplets, lipases digest the lipids, and micelles form.
Lipids end up as monoglycerides and fatty acids, which are absorbed by **diffusion** and reassembled into **triglycerides** inside the epithelial cells.
The triglycerides are packaged as chylomicrons that leave the cell and enter the lacteal, the lymph vessel of the villus.

boxes.text: Amino acids and sugars enter capillaries that drain through the hepatic portal system, so they reach the liver first. Fats take a different road: they are packaged as chylomicrons and enter the lacteal, which is a lymph vessel.
Two roads out of the gut: sugars and amino acids take the blood road (capillary, then the liver); fats take the lymph road (lacteal).

The cecum is listed SEPARATELY from the colon (slide 21): the colon is only ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid. Amino acids and monosaccharides = active transport, but lipids (monoglycerides and fatty acids) = diffusion (slides 22-23). Vitamins and minerals are NOT 'all by osmosis': only water is (slide 22). Slide 21 text says the anal sphincters are 'of either smooth or skeletal muscle'; the figure labels internal = smooth, external = skeletal.

sourceNotes: Slides 21-23. Slide 21 figure labels: transverse, ascending and descending colon, cecum, appendix, ileocecal valve, rectum, sigmoid colon, internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle), external anal sphincter (skeletal muscle), anal canal, anus. Slide 22 figure: amino acids and monosaccharides by active transport into the capillary (to hepatic portal system). Slide 23 figure steps 1-7: fat globules + bile salts, emulsion droplets, digestion by lipases, micelles, bile salts and lecithin released, triglyceride (with protein), chylomicrons, lacteal.
Trick box 'two roads' is a plain-language memory aid (outside source).

images.alt: The large intestine with the cecum, appendix, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anus and anal sphincters labelled.
A cell layer lining the intestine with carbohydrates and proteins digested outside it and amino acids and sugars crossing the cells into a capillary.

sections.title: Regulating digestion

steps.title: Nerves and hormones
bullets: Digestion is regulated by the **endocrine** (hormone) and **nervous** systems. They change how fast the gut moves and how much it secretes.
Stomach stretching triggers a neural reflex that increases peristalsis. It also stimulates the release of **gastrin**, a hormone that increases gastric juice secretion.

steps.title: Signals from the small intestine
bullets: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum triggers the release of **secretin**, a hormone that stimulates secretion from the pancreas.
Fat and protein content stimulate the secretion of **CCK** (cholecystokinin), a hormone that stimulates both the release of bile from the gallbladder and secretion from the pancreas.
Stretching of the small intestine inhibits stomach motility.

boxes.text: Each signal is a message about what has arrived. A stretched stomach says 'more juice and movement', acid in the duodenum and fat and protein in the duodenum say 'send pancreatic juice and bile', and a stretched small intestine tells the stomach to slow down.
Gastrin goes with Gastric juice. Secretin is triggered by Sour (acidic) chyme. CCK is triggered by fat and protein and is the one that also squeezes out bile from the gallbladder.

Both secretin AND CCK stimulate secretion from the pancreas (slide 24); only CCK also stimulates bile release from the gallbladder. Only gastrin increases gastric juice secretion. Stomach stretch increases peristalsis, but small intestine stretch INHIBITS stomach motility. Do not swap the triggers: acidic chyme = secretin, fat and protein = CCK.

head: Signal
Trigger
Effect
rows: Stimulates release of bile from the gallbladder and secretion from the pancreas

sourceNotes: Slide 24 (text only, no figure). The link between the signals and the needs they meet (why box) and the 'sour' memory aid are plain-language additions (outside source). The slide does not say why small intestine stretch slows the stomach.

sections.title: The gut microbiome and the gut-brain axis

steps.title: What the microbiome does
bullets: The **intestinal microbiome** is an ecological community of microorganisms living in the gut.
It defends against pathogens by acting as a physical barrier and by producing antimicrobial chemicals.
It helps digest otherwise indigestible foods (for example fibre) and synthesizes vitamins (for example K, B₆ and biotin).

steps.title: Who lives in the gut
bullets: Different species of fungi, bacteria and archaea colonize every part of the GI tract, including the stomach.
The microbiome also includes viruses, for example bacteriophages.

steps.title: How the microbiome forms
bullets: The first gut microbiome depends on how the baby is delivered. Vaginal delivery gives faster colonization that resembles vaginal flora (*Lactobacillus*, *Bacteroides*).
C-section delivery gives slower colonization that resembles skin flora (*Staphylococcus*).
Later colonization comes from the environment and diet (breast-feeding and the start of solid food). The microbiome may begin to form in utero.

steps.title: The gut-brain axis
bullets: Increasing evidence suggests the brain may be influenced by the gut microbiome through the **gut-brain axis**.
Germ-free mice overreact to stress (they have higher levels of circulating stress hormones). It is harder to apply this to humans because human behaviour is more complex.

Gut microbes can make neurotransmitters (serotonin, dopamine) and cytokines (proteins that regulate inflammation). These can enter the bloodstream and cross the blood-brain barrier, and microbial products may also modulate microglia.

boxes.text: A community that already fills the gut surface and makes its own antimicrobial chemicals leaves less room for harmful invaders. That is how the microbiome defends against pathogens.
Picture the microbiome as a garden inside the tube: it keeps weeds (pathogens) out, helps break down tough plant food (fibre) and makes some vitamins as a crop.

Slide 2 says humans themselves make only vitamin D, while slide 25 says gut microbes make K, B6 and biotin: both are true. The stomach is colonized too (slide 25). Slide 27 is cautious: 'increasing evidence suggests', 'may', 'possible'; the mouse findings do not translate directly to humans, so never say the microbiome is proven to control human behaviour.

sourceNotes: Slides 25-27 (text only). Slide 26: delivery mode, vaginal flora vs skin flora, later colonization, in utero. Slide 27: germ-free mice, neurotransmitters, cytokines, blood-brain barrier, microglia.
Why box (less room for invaders) and the garden analogy are plain-language additions (outside source).

sections.title: Building the gut tube

img.alt: A chart of how embryo tissues branch into body structures, with arrows pointing to the notochord and to splanchnic mesoderm.

steps.title: Where gut tissues come from
bullets: The **endoderm** forms the epithelium (lining) of the digestive tube.
The smooth muscle layers that drive peristalsis come from **splanchnic mesoderm**, a derivative of mesoderm. The chart places it under lateral plate mesoderm.
**Neural crest cells** form the enteric ganglia and are needed for the proper formation of the GI tract tissue layers.

img.alt: Four stages of an embryo showing the gut tube forming, with the foregut, midgut, hindgut and the two intestinal portals labelled.

steps.title: The primitive gut closes up
bullets: Endoderm folds inward (invaginates) at both ends of the embryo, the anterior and the posterior.
The portals this creates, the anterior intestinal portal (**AIP**) and the caudal intestinal portal (**CIP**), migrate toward each other. This internalizes the endoderm into a tube.
The picture labels the tube regions foregut, midgut and hindgut.

img.alt: A drawing of the gut tube coloured by region from esophagus and stomach down to small intestine, colon and rectum, with the liver and pancreas alongside.

steps.title: Regions and gut looping
bullets: The gut tube is **polarized** along the anterior-posterior axis, from esophagus to rectum. Different genes are expressed in the endoderm to specify the different regions.
Splanchnic mesoderm forms the **dorsal mesentery**, which connects the gut to the body wall.
The endoderm grows while it is connected to the body wall, so the tube buckles and folds in a predictable way. This is **gut looping**.

img.alt: Cross sections of the developing gut tube showing the endoderm in the centre, the inner circular muscle layer forming first and the outer longitudinal layer forming later.

steps.title: Smooth muscle and villi form
bullets: Splanchnic mesoderm surrounds the endoderm. In a middle zone, away from the endoderm, it becomes smooth muscle cells (the inner layer).
Migrated neural crest cells and the inner muscle cells let the surrounding mesoderm form an outer smooth muscle layer.
Smooth muscle cells compress the endoderm, which makes it buckle and form villi.

boxes.text: Villi form because of a squeeze from outside. The smooth muscle that develops around the endoderm compresses it, so the lining buckles into folds. The tube also loops because the endoderm keeps growing while it is tied to the body wall by the mesentery.
Match the first letters: Endoderm = Epithelium (lining); Splanchnic mesoderm = Smooth muscle; Neural crest = Nerves (enteric ganglia).

Do not swap the tissues: enteric ganglia come from neural crest cells, NOT mesoderm, and the epithelium comes from endoderm, NOT splanchnic mesoderm (slide 28). The slide 28 chart puts splanchnic mesoderm under lateral plate mesoderm and the notochord under chordamesoderm (the arrows highlight these two). CIP and AIP are the PORTALS that migrate toward each other, not the foregut or hindgut themselves. The slide 31 picture also shows BMP, Shh and BMP antagonist signals; the slide text does not discuss them.

sections.title: Building the liver, gallbladder and pancreas

img.alt: A 26-day embryo with the heart field next to the foregut, and a close-up of foregut endoderm turning into liver and pancreas.

steps.title: The liver bud
bullets: The **hepatic diverticulum** (liver bud) buds off the endoderm and extends out from the foregut. It branches and multiplies to make the glandular liver epithelium.
The neighbouring **cardiogenic mesoderm** (the heart field) first induces (signals) the endoderm to form the liver.
A branch of the bile duct forms the gallbladder.

img.alt: Four stages from day 30 to day 42 showing the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds growing together next to the liver bud, gallbladder and duodenum.

steps.title: The pancreas from two buds
bullets: Two separate buds, a dorsal and a ventral diverticulum, fuse to form the pancreas.
The adjacent **notochord** induces the endoderm to form the pancreas.
Only the ventral pancreatic duct remains functional in humans.

boxes.text: Nearby tissues give the signal. The heart field (cardiogenic mesoderm) lies next to the future liver and induces it, and the notochord lies next to the future pancreas and induces it. Induces means it signals the endoderm to become that organ.
Liver is next to the Heart field (cardiogenic mesoderm); Pancreas is induced by the notochord (P and N). Gallbladder = a branch off the bile duct.

Do not swap the inducers: cardiogenic mesoderm induces the LIVER (slide 32), notochord induces the PANCREAS (slide 33). Slide 33 says only the ventral pancreatic duct remains functional in humans, but the day 42 picture still labels an accessory pancreatic duct and a main pancreatic duct. Use the slide's statement.

table.title: Digestive organs at a glance
head: Organ
Main jobs
What it secretes or adds
rows: Chewing (mechanical digestion); starts digestion of starch
Stores and mixes food; begins protein digestion; regulates delivery to the small intestine
Hydrochloric acid, intrinsic factor, mucus, pepsinogen
Digestion and absorption (about 90% of food is absorbed)
Intestinal enzymes; also receives bile and pancreatic juice
Endocrine (blood glucose) and exocrine (pancreatic juice) functions
Sodium bicarbonate, trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, pancreatic amylase, lipase, nucleases
Produces bile; processes and stores nutrients
Absorbs the last of the water and nutrients; stores and eliminates waste

cards.front: What are essential nutrients?
cards.back: Nutrients that can only be obtained in the diet: essential fatty acids (linoleic and linolenic acid), essential amino acids (histidine, isoleucine, methionine), vitamins (humans can synthesize only vitamin D) and minerals (iron, sodium, iodine, zinc, manganese, molybdenum).
cards.short: Nutrients only obtainable from the diet

cards.front: What is the alimentary canal (GI tract), and what is the lumen?
cards.back: The alimentary canal is the hollow tube through the body: mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus. It makes humans doughnut-shaped, and the space inside the tube is the lumen.
cards.short: Hollow tube from mouth to anus

cards.front: Which organs are the accessory organs of the GI system?
cards.back: The salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas. They are not part of the tube, but they add secretions that help digestion.

cards.front: What are the four layers of the GI wall from the lumen outward, and what does each do?
cards.back: Mucosa (mucous membrane lining the lumen), submucosa (connective tissue with blood vessels, lymph vessels and nerves), muscularis (smooth muscle that moves food) and serosa (outer connective tissue that anchors the tract through the mesentery).

cards.front: What are sphincters?
cards.back: Thick muscular rings that separate some of the organs along the GI tract, such as the esophageal sphincter, the pyloric sphincter and the anal sphincters.

cards.front: What is peristalsis?
cards.back: A GI motility that propels a bolus forward. The muscle in front of the bolus relaxes while the muscle behind it contracts, which pushes the bolus on.
cards.short: Muscle waves that push food forward

cards.front: What is segmentation?
cards.back: A GI motility that mixes food. Sections of smooth muscle relax and contract randomly, giving a back-and-forth mixing motion that presses food against the mucosa so nutrients can be absorbed.

cards.front: How does digestion begin in the mouth?
cards.back: Chewing (mastication) is mechanical digestion. Saliva from three pairs of exocrine salivary glands contains salivary amylase, which digests starch (chemical digestion).
cards.short: Chewing plus salivary amylase on starch

cards.front: What happens in the voluntary phase of swallowing?
cards.back: The tongue voluntarily pushes the bolus into the pharynx while the esophagus remains closed.
cards.short: Tongue pushes bolus into the pharynx

cards.front: What happens in the involuntary phase of swallowing?
cards.back: The soft palate raises to close the passage to the nasal cavity, and the epiglottis bends to close the trachea and open the esophagus. The bolus then moves down the esophagus to the stomach, past the esophageal sphincter.

cards.front: What does hydrochloric acid do in the stomach, and which cells make it?
cards.back: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid. It is highly acidic (about pH 2) and breaks down large bits of food.
cards.short: Acid from parietal cells, pH about 2

cards.front: What is intrinsic factor?
cards.back: A substance secreted by parietal cells that facilitates the absorption of vitamin B₁₂ in the small intestine.

cards.front: What protects the stomach lining from the acid?
cards.back: Mucus. Mucin is secreted by the mucous neck cells, and the mucus protects the stomach lining from being degraded by the acid.

cards.front: What are pepsinogen and pepsin?
cards.back: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen. In the low-pH stomach it is converted into pepsin, which begins protein digestion.
cards.short: Chief cell product activated by low pH

cards.front: Why do the stomach contents churn during peristalsis?
cards.back: Because of the pyloric sphincter at the exit of the stomach. Only some chyme slowly leaks through it into the small intestine.

cards.front: What does the small intestine do?
cards.back: It digests and absorbs. It neutralizes stomach acid, adds digestive enzymes and bile, and breaks proteins, carbohydrates and lipids into absorbable materials. About 90% of food is absorbed there.
cards.short: Digestion and absorption, about 90% of food

cards.front: Name the three parts of the small intestine and their main jobs.
cards.back: The duodenum is where most digestion occurs. The jejunum and the ileum are for absorption.
cards.short: Duodenum digests; jejunum and ileum absorb

cards.front: How does the small intestine increase its surface area?
cards.back: Large folds are covered with microscopic villi, which are made of epithelial cells covered in microvilli. Each villus has blood vessels and a central lymph vessel called the lacteal.

cards.front: What is celiac disease?
cards.back: Gluten proteins bind to mutated antigen-presenting receptors and trigger an immune response and inflammation in the small intestine. The villi are damaged and shrink, leading to malabsorption and nutrient deficiency. About 1% of people have it and the only treatment is a gluten-free diet.
cards.short: Gluten damages villi and causes malabsorption

cards.front: What are the two functions of the pancreas?
cards.back: Endocrine (regulation of blood glucose levels) and exocrine (secretion of pancreatic juice).

cards.front: What does pancreatic juice contain?
cards.back: Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃), which neutralizes stomach acid, and digestive enzymes: trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase (proteins), pancreatic amylase (starch), lipase (lipids) and pancreatic nucleases (DNA and RNA).
cards.short: Bicarbonate plus enzymes for all nutrients

cards.front: Which enzymes digest carbohydrates, and what do they make?
cards.back: Salivary amylase (mouth) and pancreatic amylase (small intestine) turn polysaccharides into disaccharides. Maltase (small intestine) turns disaccharides into monosaccharides such as glucose.

cards.front: Which enzymes digest proteins, and what do they make?
cards.back: Pepsin (stomach), trypsin and chymotrypsin (pancreas, small intestine) turn proteins into peptides. Carboxypeptidase (pancreas) and the intestinal enzymes turn peptides into amino acids.
cards.short: Proteins to peptides to amino acids

cards.front: What does lipase do, and where does it come from?
cards.back: Lipase is secreted by the pancreas and works in the small intestine. It digests triglycerides into free fatty acids and monoglyceride.

cards.front: What does bile do, and where is it made?
cards.back: The liver produces bile. Bile emulsifies lipids into micelles, which eases their digestion by lipase.

cards.front: What does the gallbladder do?
cards.back: It concentrates and stores bile, and delivers it to the duodenum through the common bile duct.

cards.front: What does the large intestine do, and what are its parts?
cards.back: It absorbs nutrients and water and temporarily stores and eliminates waste. Its parts are the cecum (with the appendix), the colon (ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid), the rectum and the anus, which is closed off by two anal sphincters.
cards.short: Absorbs water, stores and eliminates waste

cards.front: How are amino acids, monosaccharides, water, vitamins and minerals absorbed?
cards.back: Amino acids and monosaccharides by active transport (then into the capillary toward the hepatic portal system), water by osmosis, and vitamins and minerals by various means depending on whether they are water-soluble or fat-soluble.

cards.front: How are lipids absorbed?
cards.back: Lipids are broken down into monoglycerides and fatty acids, which are absorbed by diffusion and reassembled into triglycerides in the epithelial cells. The triglycerides are packaged as chylomicrons that enter the lacteal.

cards.front: What triggers gastrin, and what does it do?
cards.back: Stomach stretching triggers a neural reflex that increases peristalsis and stimulates the release of gastrin, a hormone that increases gastric juice secretion.

cards.front: What triggers secretin, and what does it do?
cards.back: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum triggers the release of secretin, a hormone that stimulates secretion from the pancreas.

cards.front: What triggers CCK, and what does it do?
cards.back: Fat and protein content stimulate the secretion of CCK (cholecystokinin), a hormone that stimulates both the release of bile from the gallbladder and secretion from the pancreas.

cards.front: What does the intestinal microbiome do?
cards.back: It is an ecological community of microorganisms in the gut. It defends against pathogens (physical barrier and antimicrobial chemicals), helps digest otherwise indigestible foods such as fibre, and synthesizes vitamins such as K, B₆ and biotin.

cards.front: How does the mode of delivery affect the infant gut microbiome?
cards.back: Vaginal delivery gives faster colonization that resembles vaginal flora (Lactobacillus, Bacteroides). C-section gives slower colonization that resembles skin flora (Staphylococcus). Later colonization depends on the environment and diet, and the microbiome may begin to form in utero.

cards.front: What is the gut-brain axis?
cards.back: Evidence suggests the brain may be influenced by the gut microbiome. Gut microbes can make neurotransmitters (serotonin, dopamine) and cytokines that can enter the bloodstream and cross the blood-brain barrier, but findings in germ-free mice are hard to translate to humans.
cards.short: Gut microbes may influence the brain

cards.front: What do endoderm, splanchnic mesoderm and neural crest cells form in the GI tract?
cards.back: Endoderm forms the epithelium of the digestive tube. Splanchnic mesoderm forms the smooth muscle layers (and the dorsal mesentery). Neural crest cells form the enteric ganglia and are needed for the proper formation of the tissue layers.
cards.short: Endoderm lining, mesoderm muscle, crest nerves

cards.front: How does the primitive gut form?
cards.back: Endoderm invaginates at the anterior and posterior ends of the embryo. The portals that form (CIP and AIP) migrate toward each other and internalize the endoderm.
cards.short: Portals migrate together and close the tube

cards.front: What is gut looping, and what specifies the regions of the gut?
cards.back: The gut tube is polarized along the anterior-posterior axis, and different genes expressed in the endoderm specify different regions. As the endoderm grows while connected to the body wall by the dorsal mesentery, the tube buckles and folds in a predictable way, called gut looping.
cards.short: Predictable folding of the growing gut tube

cards.front: How do the smooth muscle layers and villi develop?
cards.back: Splanchnic mesoderm becomes smooth muscle cells in a middle zone away from the endoderm, and neural crest cells with the inner muscle cells let an outer layer form. The smooth muscle cells compress the endoderm so that it buckles and forms villi.

cards.front: How do the liver, gallbladder and pancreas develop?
cards.back: The liver bud (hepatic diverticulum) buds off the foregut endoderm, induced by cardiogenic mesoderm, and a branch of the bile duct forms the gallbladder. Dorsal and ventral diverticula fuse to form the pancreas, induced by the notochord; only the ventral pancreatic duct remains functional in humans.
cards.short: Liver bud, gallbladder branch, fused pancreas buds

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the GI tract (alimentary canal) itself?
quiz.why: The GI tract is the hollow tube from mouth to anus: mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus. The gallbladder is an accessory organ (like the salivary glands, liver and pancreas) that sends its product into the tube.

quiz.q:
Which of the following statements about essential nutrients are correct?
I. Essential amino acids can only be obtained in the diet.
II. Humans can make every vitamin except vitamin D.
III. Iron, sodium and iodine are examples of essential minerals.
quiz.why: Essential nutrients can only be obtained in the diet, and iron, sodium, iodine, zinc, manganese and molybdenum are the listed minerals. Statement II is reversed: vitamin D is the only vitamin humans can synthesize themselves.

quiz.q: Which list gives the layers of the GI tract wall in order from the lumen outward?
quiz.why: The mucosa lines the lumen. Under it the submucosa holds blood vessels, lymph vessels and nerves, then comes the muscularis that moves food, and the serosa is the outer covering anchored by the mesentery.

quiz.q: The picture shows sections of the gut wall relaxing and contracting in a back-and-forth pattern. What is this movement, and what does it do?
options: Peristalsis: it pushes the bolus forward along the tract
Segmentation: it pushes the bolus forward along the tract
Peristalsis: it mixes food and presses it against the mucosa
Segmentation: it mixes food and presses it against the mucosa so nutrients can be absorbed
quiz.why: In segmentation, sections of smooth muscle relax and contract at random, which mixes food back and forth and presses it against the mucosa so that nutrients can be absorbed. Peristalsis is the movement that propels a bolus forward.

img.alt: Three views of an intestine wall pinching in several places at once so the food is split into small moving pockets.

quiz.q:
Which of the following describe peristalsis?
I. It propels a bolus of food forward.
II. The muscle behind the bolus contracts while the muscle in front of it relaxes.
III. Sections of smooth muscle relax and contract randomly to mix food.
quiz.why: Peristalsis pushes the bolus forward because the muscle behind it contracts and the muscle in front of it relaxes. Random relaxing and contracting to mix food describes segmentation.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of saliva or the salivary glands?
quiz.why: Pepsin is made in the stomach, from pepsinogen secreted by chief cells. Saliva moistens food, contains bicarbonate that maintains pH, amylase that digests starch and lysozyme that inhibits bacteria.

quiz.q: During the involuntary phase of swallowing, why must the epiglottis bend?
options: To close the passage to the nasal cavity
To push the bolus from the mouth into the pharynx
To close the esophageal sphincter so food cannot pass
To close the trachea and open the esophagus, so the bolus goes down toward the stomach
To open the trachea so air can reach the stomach
quiz.why: The epiglottis bends to close the trachea and open the esophagus at the same moment, so the bolus travels down the esophagus. The soft palate, not the epiglottis, closes the passage to the nasal cavity, and the tongue pushes the bolus into the pharynx.

quiz.q:
Which steps of swallowing are voluntary?
I. The tongue pushes the bolus into the pharynx.
II. The soft palate raises to close the passage to the nasal cavity.
III. The epiglottis bends to close the trachea.
quiz.why: Swallowing has a voluntary phase, in which the tongue pushes the bolus into the pharynx, and an involuntary phase, in which the soft palate rises and the epiglottis bends.

quiz.q: A patient's stomach has lost its parietal cells. Which result is expected?
options: Less mucus to protect the stomach lining
No pepsinogen secretion, because chief cells depend on parietal cells
More intrinsic factor and better absorption of vitamin B₁₂
A rise in salivary amylase output
Less hydrochloric acid and poorer absorption of vitamin B₁₂
quiz.why: Parietal cells secrete both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. Without them there is less acid to break down large bits of food, and without intrinsic factor the small intestine absorbs vitamin B₁₂ poorly. Mucus comes from mucous neck cells and pepsinogen from chief cells.

quiz.q: Suppose the stomach contents became much less acidic (a higher pH). What would happen to protein digestion in the stomach?
options: It would rise, because pepsinogen works best at a neutral pH
It would fall, because less pepsinogen would be converted into active pepsin
It would be unchanged, because trypsin takes over in the stomach
It would fall, because the chief cells would stop making mucus
It would be unchanged, because salivary amylase digests proteins
quiz.why: Pepsinogen is converted into pepsin in the low-pH stomach environment, and pepsin begins protein digestion. With a higher pH less pepsin would form, so stomach protein digestion would drop.

quiz.q: The picture shows peristalsis in the stomach. Which structure is responsible for the churning of the stomach contents?
quiz.why: Peristalsis churns the stomach contents because of the pyloric sphincter at the exit. Only some chyme slowly leaks through it into the small intestine.

img.alt: Four views of the stomach showing waves of muscle contraction pushing the contents toward the pyloric sphincter and back.

quiz.q: Which statement about the small intestine is INCORRECT?
options: About 90% of food is absorbed there
Most digestion occurs in the ileum
The jejunum and the ileum are for absorption
Its mucosa is folded into villi that are covered in microvilli
quiz.why: Most digestion occurs in the duodenum. The jejunum and the ileum are the parts labelled for absorption.

quiz.q: The left picture shows villi damaged by celiac disease. What is the most direct result of this damage?
options: Failure of peristalsis in the esophagus
Too much hydrochloric acid in the stomach
quiz.why: Gluten triggers an immune response and inflammation, and the villi are damaged and shrink. With less absorbing surface, nutrients are absorbed poorly (malabsorption) and a deficiency follows. The only treatment is a gluten-free diet.

img.alt: The lining of a small intestine with damaged flat villi on the left and normal finger-like villi on the right.

quiz.q: Where is pepsin active, and what does it produce?
options: In the small intestine, where it turns peptides into amino acids
In the mouth, where it turns polysaccharides into disaccharides
In the small intestine, where it turns proteins into peptides
In the stomach, where it turns peptides into amino acids
In the stomach, where it turns proteins into peptides
quiz.why: Pepsin is made in the stomach and is active in the stomach, where it breaks proteins into peptides. Trypsin and chymotrypsin do the same job in the small intestine, and carboxypeptidase and the intestinal enzymes make amino acids from peptides.

quiz.q: Which pair of enzymes, in order, converts starch (a polysaccharide) into glucose?
quiz.why: Amylase (salivary or pancreatic) turns polysaccharides into disaccharides. Maltase in the small intestine then turns disaccharides into monosaccharides such as glucose.

quiz.q:
Which of the following does the pancreas secrete to help digestion?
I. Sodium bicarbonate, which neutralizes stomach acid
II. Pancreatic amylase, which digests starch
III. Pepsin, which digests proteins
quiz.why: Pancreatic juice contains sodium bicarbonate and enzymes such as trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, pancreatic amylase, lipase and nucleases. Pepsin comes from the stomach.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of bile in fat digestion?
options: It emulsifies lipids into micelles, which eases their digestion by lipase
It chemically splits triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglyceride
It neutralizes acidic chyme in the duodenum
It is made in the gallbladder and stored in the liver
It digests DNA and RNA in the small intestine
quiz.why: The liver produces bile and the gallbladder concentrates and stores it. Bile emulsifies lipids into micelles, which eases digestion by lipase; lipase from the pancreas does the chemical splitting, and sodium bicarbonate does the neutralizing.

quiz.q: In the picture, where do amino acids and monosaccharides go after they cross the epithelial cell layer?
options: Into the lacteal, packaged as chylomicrons
Into the capillary, toward the hepatic portal system and the liver
Straight to the gallbladder for storage
Into the stomach through the pyloric sphincter
quiz.why: Amino acids and monosaccharides are absorbed by active transport and pass into the capillary, which leads toward the hepatic portal system (the liver). Fats take a different route, through the lacteal.

img.alt: A cell layer lining the intestine with carbohydrates and proteins digested outside it and amino acids and sugars crossing the cells into a capillary.

quiz.q: In the picture, what happens to triglycerides after they are reassembled inside the epithelial cell?
options: They are actively transported into the capillary toward the hepatic portal system
They return to the lumen as micelles with bile salts
They are digested again by pepsin
They are packaged into chylomicrons that leave the cell and enter the lacteal
They are emulsified by bile salts inside the cell
quiz.why: Monoglycerides and fatty acids diffuse into the epithelial cell and are reassembled into triglycerides. The triglycerides, with protein, form chylomicrons that pass into the lacteal, the lymph vessel of the villus.

img.alt: Seven numbered steps of fat digestion from fat globules and bile salts to chylomicrons entering the lacteal.

quiz.q: Which of the following pairings of nutrient and absorption method is INCORRECT?
options: Vitamins and minerals: all absorbed by osmosis
quiz.why: Vitamins and minerals are absorbed by various means, depending on whether they are water-soluble or fat-soluble. Only water is absorbed by osmosis.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four divisions of the colon?
quiz.why: The colon is divided into the ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon. The cecum (with the appendix) is listed as a separate part of the large intestine, followed by the colon, the rectum and the anus.

quiz.q: The anus is closed off from the outside by two anal sphincters. According to the picture, which statement is correct?
options: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle and the external sphincter is skeletal muscle
The internal sphincter is skeletal muscle and the external sphincter is smooth muscle
The anus has only one sphincter, made of smooth muscle
quiz.why: The picture labels the internal anal sphincter as smooth muscle and the external anal sphincter as skeletal muscle. The text says the two anal sphincters are made of either smooth or skeletal muscle.

img.alt: The large intestine with the cecum, appendix, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anus and anal sphincters labelled.

quiz.q: A meal rich in fat and protein reaches the small intestine. Which hormone is released, and what does it do?
options: Gastrin: it increases gastric juice secretion
Secretin: it stimulates release of bile from the gallbladder
CCK (cholecystokinin): it stimulates release of bile from the gallbladder and secretion from the pancreas
Secretin: it increases peristalsis in the stomach
quiz.why: Fat and protein content stimulate CCK, which stimulates both the release of bile from the gallbladder and secretion from the pancreas. Gastrin acts after the stomach stretches, and secretin is triggered by acidic chyme.

quiz.q:
Which of the following statements about gastrin are correct?
I. It is released after the stomach stretches.
II. It increases gastric juice secretion.
III. It is released when acidic chyme enters the duodenum.
quiz.why: Stomach stretching triggers a neural reflex that increases peristalsis and stimulates the release of gastrin, which increases gastric juice secretion. Acidic chyme entering the duodenum triggers secretin instead.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the intestinal microbiome?
options: Defending against pathogens by acting as a physical barrier
Helping digest otherwise indigestible foods such as fibre
Synthesizing vitamins such as K, B₆ and biotin
quiz.why: Bile is produced by the liver. The microbiome defends against pathogens (as a barrier and with antimicrobial chemicals), helps digest foods such as fibre and synthesizes vitamins K, B₆ and biotin.

quiz.q: An infant's gut bacteria were slow to colonize and resemble skin flora, such as Staphylococcus. Which delivery is most likely?
options: Any delivery, because the delivery mode does not affect the first gut bacteria
Vaginal delivery, because Staphylococcus resembles vaginal flora
Neither, because the gut microbiome only starts when solid food is introduced
quiz.why: C-section delivery gives slower colonization with a composition resembling skin flora (for example Staphylococcus). Vaginal delivery gives faster colonization resembling vaginal flora (for example Lactobacillus and Bacteroides).

quiz.q: Which statement about the gut-brain axis is best supported?
options: Findings in mice have been proven to apply directly to human behaviour
Germ-free mice show lower levels of circulating stress hormones
Gut microbes can make neurotransmitters such as serotonin and dopamine, and cytokines, that can enter the bloodstream and cross the blood-brain barrier
The brain influences the gut microbiome, but the microbiome never influences the brain
quiz.why: Evidence suggests the brain may be influenced by the gut microbiome. Germ-free mice overreact to stress, but direct translation to humans is hard because human behaviour is more complex, and microbial metabolites may modulate microglial functions.

quiz.q: Which pairing of embryonic tissue and GI structure is correct?
options: Splanchnic mesoderm: epithelium of the digestive tube
quiz.why: Endoderm forms the epithelium, splanchnic mesoderm forms the smooth muscle layers, and neural crest cells form the enteric ganglia. Cardiogenic mesoderm induces the liver and the notochord induces the pancreas.

quiz.q:
Which of the following statements about gut development are correct?
I. Smooth muscle cells compress the endoderm, causing it to buckle and form villi.
II. The notochord induces the endoderm to form the pancreas.
III. Gut looping happens as the endoderm grows while connected to the body wall.
quiz.why: All three statements are true. The muscle squeezes the lining into villi, the adjacent notochord induces the pancreas, and the tube folds in a predictable way because it grows while tied to the body wall.

quiz.q: An adult has 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars. How many teeth is that in total?
quiz.why: Add the four types: 8 + 4 + 8 + 12 = 32 adult teeth.
quiz.source: Slide 9 (tooth counts from the figure; the total is a sum)

order.title: The path of food through the GI tract
order.prompt: Put the parts of the GI tract in the order food passes through them, from the first to the last.
order.why: Food enters at the mouth and is swallowed through the pharynx and esophagus. It is mixed in the stomach, digested and mostly absorbed in the small intestine, then passes through the large intestine and leaves through the rectum and the anus.

order.title: Layers of the GI wall
order.prompt: Put the layers in order from the space inside the tube to the outside of the wall.
order.why: The mucosa touches the lumen, the submucosa under it holds blood vessels, lymph vessels and nerves, the muscularis is the smooth muscle that moves food, and the serosa is the outermost covering.

order.title: From the mouth to the stomach
order.prompt: Put the steps in the order they happen as food is chewed and swallowed.
order.why: Chewing and saliva begin digestion in the mouth. The voluntary phase of swallowing comes first, when the tongue pushes the bolus into the pharynx. Then the involuntary phase closes the nasal passage and the airway, and the bolus travels down the esophagus past the esophageal sphincter into the stomach.
order.topLabel: End: food is in the stomach
order.bottomLabel: Start: food is in the mouth

layers.name: Chewing and saliva begin digestion in the mouth
The tongue pushes the bolus into the pharynx (voluntary)
The soft palate rises and the epiglottis bends (involuntary)
The bolus moves down the esophagus
The bolus passes the esophageal sphincter into the stomach

order.title: How fat is digested and absorbed
order.prompt: Put the steps of fat digestion and absorption in order, from the first step to the last.
order.why: Bile salts break fat globules into emulsion droplets, lipases digest the lipids and micelles form. Monoglycerides and fatty acids diffuse into the epithelial cell and are reassembled into triglycerides. These are packaged as chylomicrons, which enter the lacteal.

layers.name: Fat globules meet bile salts and form emulsion droplets
Monoglycerides and fatty acids diffuse into the epithelial cell
Triglycerides are reassembled in the cell

sort.title: Tract or accessory organ?
sort.prompt: Sort each organ into a part of the GI tract or an accessory organ.
sort.why: The GI tract is the hollow tube from mouth to anus. The accessory organs (salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas) are not part of the tube, but they add secretions that help digestion.

sort.title: Which nutrient does the enzyme digest?
sort.prompt: Sort each enzyme by the kind of food molecule it digests.
sort.why: Amylases and maltase act on starch and sugars, pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase and the intestinal enzymes act on proteins and peptides, lipase acts on triglycerides, and the nucleases and nucleosidases act on DNA and RNA.

sort.title: Gastrin, secretin or CCK?
sort.prompt: Sort each description into the hormone it belongs to.

items.text: Works alongside a neural reflex that increases peristalsis
Released when acidic chyme enters the duodenum
Stimulates secretion from the pancreas after acidic chyme arrives
Released in response to fat and protein content
Stimulates release of bile from the gallbladder

sort.why: Gastrin goes with the stretched stomach and gastric juice, secretin goes with acidic chyme and the pancreas, and CCK goes with fat and protein and is the one that also makes the gallbladder release bile.
